tldr: Changing an upper-body manipulation policy should never require retraining the locomotion and balance controller. DUET completely excludes the arm joints from the lower-body reinforcement learning locomotion policy's action space, combining commands only at the robot's transmission interface. With this loosely coupled architecture, the authors demonstrate that different VLA models can be swapped in on the fly using the exact same locomotion policy.
hero_caption: System architecture diagram of DUET. Top: In simulation, reinforcement learning trains the locomotion policy under an arm pose curriculum and dynamics randomization. Bottom: During hardware deployment, the locomotion process (13 lower-body joints) and manipulation process (10 arm joints) run independently, and their commands combine only in the final transmission message.
overview:
When making a humanoid robot perform tasks while moving (loco-manipulation), most existing studies use whole-body control, training all joints together in a single network. However, this approach creates a tight coupling. If you want to change the task or the arm manipulation policy, you must retrain or redesign the locomotion controller that keeps the robot balanced.

To solve this, the authors propose DUET, a framework that completely decouples upper- and lower-body control. The idea is simple. The arm joints are completely excluded from the action space of the lower-body reinforcement learning policy. Instead, the arm states are received purely as observations—treated as external disturbances. Arm joint targets are streamed directly from a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model or similar source, and are merely combined when assembling the lowest-level motor command message.

In hardware experiments on a 23-DOF Unitree G1, the robot successfully performed produce grasping and carrying tasks by swapping between two distinct VLA models (GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5) without any retraining or restarting, using the exact same locomotion checkpoint. In simulation evaluations, it maintained stable tracking with zero falls. Ablation studies revealed that the upper-body pose curriculum plays a decisive role in keeping the robot upright. While there is a cost in trunk tilt because the arms cannot be used for momentum control, DUET demonstrates high modularity that allows rapidly evolving foundation models to be paired immediately with a mobile base.
contributions: Developed a reinforcement learning locomotion policy on a 23-DOF Unitree G1 that tracks planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from 0.18 m to 0.73 m.
Built a decoupled execution interface that excludes arm joints from the locomotion policy's action space, enabling arbitrary manipulation policies to be swapped without retraining or restarting.
Deployed two different modern VLA models (GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5) zero-shot on hardware under the exact same locomotion checkpoint.

Pinpointed via detailed ablations that the upper-body pose curriculum is dominant for stability, and quantified the posture-maintenance cost (trunk tilt) of decoupling through comparisons with whole-body control.

sections.heading: Why Should Changing the Arm Policy Force You to Retrain Walking?
sections.summary: In humanoid loco-manipulation, the dependency requiring locomotion retraining whenever the manipulation policy changes has been a persistent challenge. DUET treats the lower body as an autonomous stabilization base, proposing a decoupled framework independent of any arm manipulation policy.
sections.details:
Humanoid robots are expected to manipulate objects at varying heights while moving. For instance, transporting produce between workstations or picking fruit from low stands requires a coordinated sequence: approaching the target, crouching down, recognizing the object, and grasping it.

However, most prior loco-manipulation works have relied on whole-body control, optimizing all joints simultaneously with a single policy. While these achieve high coordination, they impose a severe constraint: whenever the manipulation task or policy changes, the locomotion controller must be retrained or readapted.

Another path is decoupled control between the legs and arms. Existing decoupled systems have driven the arms via exoskeleton teleoperation cockpits or inverse kinematics (IK) solvers. The authors take this a step further: what moves the arms should be any pretrained policy (such as a VLA), and exchanging it should incur zero cost on the locomotion side.

DUET (Decoupled Upper- and Lower-Body Execution) runs an RL locomotion policy and a VLA manipulation policy concurrently on a 23-DOF Unitree G1. The two policies share only the physical robot body, combining commands only at the lowest layer of control messages. This delivers modularity where independently developed manipulation foundation models can be swapped and executed without modifying the locomotion controller at all.

sections.heading: Whole-Body or Decoupled? Contextualizing with Prior Work
sections.summary: The authors review RL locomotion, whole-body coordination, decoupled loco-manipulation, and advances in VLA models. DUET is the only system that passes arm target commands straight through without modification while allowing manipulation policies to be swapped.
sections.details:
### Reinforcement Learning for Locomotion and Whole-Body Trends
Combining massively parallel simulation with PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) quickly expanded from quadrupedal robots to real-world humanoid walking. This work follows that trend, using a GPU-parallelized MuJoCo-based environment (mjlab/MuJoCo Playground) instead of Isaac Gym to achieve comparable parallel training scale.

Meanwhile, for humanoid loco-manipulation, whole-body policies like EWBC, HumanPlus, OmniH2O, and HOVER have been mainstream. Because they train arms and legs in a shared representation space, they exhibit excellent coordination. However, since arm behavior is baked inside the controller, flexibly swapping the manipulation policy alone is difficult.

### Decoupled Systems and VLA Integration
In contrast, decoupled controllers like HOMIE and GR00T separate the legs and arms. HOMIE used an exoskeleton cockpit, and GR00T drove the arms with an IK solver. DUET adopts three training ingredients proposed by HOMIE—an upper-body pose curriculum, a height-tracking reward, and mirror symmetry. However, it replaces the fixed arm-command sources with a pretrained VLA model that has no awareness of the lower body.

VLA models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, the pi series, and GR00T N1 are typically trained on stationary, fixed-base setups. DUET treats these models as black boxes outputting joint targets. By training the legs to withstand their physical effects, it deploys them onto bipedal humanoids without rewriting the model.

sections.heading: All It Takes to Connect Upper and Lower Body Is Merging Messages
sections.summary: The hardware is a 23-DOF Unitree G1. The locomotion policy controls 12 leg joints and 1 waist yaw joint, while the manipulation policy handles 10 arm joints. The locomotion process acts as the sole motor command sender, merging arm commands from a separate process in an extremely decoupled architecture.
sections.details:
### Hardware Setup
The experimental platform is a 23-DOF Unitree G1. It has 6 joints per leg (12 total), 1 waist yaw joint, and 5 joints per arm (10 total). Both wrists are equipped with Unitree Dex3-1 3-finger hands (approx. 810 g per assembly), an Intel RealSense D455 on the head, and a D405 on the right wrist as an in-hand camera.

### Training and Export
The locomotion policy is trained in parallel simulation against an arm pose curriculum and randomized dynamics. The resulting model is exported to ONNX format. Crucially, the ONNX file embeds joint order, PD gains, action scales, observation layout, command ranges, and their hashes as metadata. This provides a "self-describing" contract that prevents unintended runaway behavior caused by deployment misconfigurations.

### Hardware Deployment Pipeline
On the workstation, two independent processes run via Ethernet (DDS communication):
- Locomotion process (50 Hz): Reads all 23 joint states, builds a 71-dimensional observation, and infers target offsets for the 13 lower-body joints. It copies the latest 10 arm joint commands and PD gains received from the manipulation process, and solely publishes the merged command to the robot's onboard PD controller (200 Hz).
- Manipulation process (~15 Hz): The VLA model autonomously infers arm joint target chunks from images and text, publishing them to a dedicated topic.

If communication from the manipulation process drops, the locomotion process holds the last received targets. Arm delays or stalls never halt leg control. The locomotion policy needs no knowledge of the arm policy's identity—it merely observes arm joint positions and velocities. This makes the manipulation model completely interchangeable.

captions.P6: Overall system architecture. The locomotion policy trained in the parallel simulation at top is exported to ONNX. At bottom, on the workstation, the locomotion process and VLA manipulation process run completely independently, demonstrating the loose coupling.

sections.heading: From Deep Crouching to Upright Standing: Training the Lower-Body Policy
sections.summary: The locomotion policy runs at 50 Hz, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height. A dynamic arm pose curriculum, a 20-term reward function, mirror symmetry augmentation, and thorough domain randomization give it robust resilience against unseen upper-body motions.
sections.details:
### Observation and Action Design
The input to the locomotion policy is a 71-dimensional observation vector. It includes base angular velocity, projected gravity, 3D velocity commands, a 2D gait phase clock, positions and velocities of all 23 joints, the previous 13D action, and commanded pelvis height. Arm joint states are included as a 20D observation, but are completely absent from the action (output). The policy outputs target position offsets only for the 13 lower-body joints (12 leg joints and 1 waist yaw joint).

### Commands and Crouching Motions
Commands are resampled every 3 to 8 seconds, providing planar velocity, turning rate, and a wide pelvis height range from 0.18 m to 0.73 m. Deep crouching is commanded only when stationary; during locomotion, height is restricted to 0.60 m or above for safety.

### Upper-Body Pose Curriculum
During training, the arms are driven not by a policy, but by a random disturbance generator. New target poses are sampled and interpolated roughly every 1 second (50 steps). 70% of targets are sampled around 6 manipulation "anchor poses" (holding a box at waist height, holding a box at chest height, reaching forward, crouching while reaching low, reaching high, and resting). The remaining 30% are sampled uniformly across the workspace. A curriculum gradually scales up the amplitude of these arm motions from zero early in training.

### Rewards, Symmetry, and Domain Randomization
The reward consists of 20 terms covering velocity and height tracking, upright posture maintenance, gait pattern shaping, joint limits, and collision penalties. A schedule relaxes knee and ankle posture regularization tolerances at lower heights so as not to impede crouching. Sagittal mirror symmetry is incorporated via data augmentation and consistency loss. Furthermore, wide domain randomization is applied during training: foot friction (0.3 to 1.6), base center of mass, hand payload (up to +1.75 kg per hand), torso payload, and push disturbances (up to 0.7 m/s).

captions.P7: Demonstration of independence between pelvis height commands and arm pose commands on hardware. From left to right: standing, half-crouching, and fully crouching. The upper row keeps arms in a rest position, while the lower row maintains the same forward reach pose, achieving stable balance at each height.
captions.P8: Walking strides at two different pelvis heights. The top row shows walking at upright height, while the bottom row shows walking in a crouched state at a pelvis height of 0.60 m. Stable periodic gaits are achieved even with deeply bent knees.

sections.heading: Running GR00T and pi0.5 Zero-Shot on the Locomotion Layer
sections.summary: Two distinct VLA models (GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5) were run on the exact same locomotion checkpoint without any policy modifications. Arm commands are transmitted transparently to the robot via rate limiting.
sections.details:
### Transparent Command Interface
The exported locomotion policy is loaded into a C++ controller. Arm joint targets arrive over a dedicated topic and are considered active if a message arrived within the last 200 ms. Targets transition with a 20 rad/s rate limit, which is practically transparent and latency-free for the VLA. In addition, the P and D gains for arm joints directly adopt the values in the manipulation message, giving the manipulation policy full control over its own end-effector compliance.

### Hardware Validation with Two Distinct VLAs
In this study, two VLA models with completely different architectures were run on the same locomotion checkpoint:
- GR00T N1.7: Uses Cosmos-Reason2-2B as backbone. With the backbone frozen, only the action head was fine-tuned for 10,000 steps on 605 episodes of produce-handling data collected on the same robot.
- pi0.5: Adapted for 22,000 steps using LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) on the same 605-episode dataset.

Crucially, both models were trained on fixed-base (stationary) data and had no awareness of the lower-body locomotion policy. From the locomotion side, only the process issuing arm targets changed. It required no retraining, nor even a process restart.

sections.heading: Hardware and Simulation Experiments: Performance, Ablations, and Comparison with Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: In simulation evaluations, DUET achieved zero falls, 0.186 m/s linear velocity error, and 0.016 m height error. Ablations highlighted the vital importance of the arm curriculum. Hardware tests confirmed successful payload carrying and pick-and-place tasks, while quantifying the cost of decoupling: roughly 8 degrees more trunk tilt than whole-body control.
sections.details:
### Deployment Policy Performance and Checkpoint Selection
In a 1024-environment simulation evaluation, the deployed policy achieved a linear velocity error of 0.186 m/s, an angular velocity error of 0.142 rad/s, and a height error of 0.016 m. It suffered zero falls over 20-second episodes (fall rate of 0.00 falls/env-minute). Notably, checkpoint selection picked the best checkpoint strictly ranked by fall rate and tracking errors rather than defaulting to the final training iteration.

### Findings from Ablation Studies
Leave-one-out ablations clarified the role of each training element:
- Removing the arm pose curriculum: This was the most catastrophic. Episode survival dropped from 20.0 s to 7.4 s, fall rate spiked to 6.06 per env-minute, and velocity tracking error more than doubled.
- Removing height commands: Survival fell to 11.1 s, with a fall rate of 2.67 per env-minute.
- Removing mirror symmetry: Survival and fall rate were unaffected, but symmetry loss surged and tracking error deteriorated by 12% to 40%. Thus, symmetry contributes to gait elegance and tracking accuracy rather than fall prevention.

### Operational Limits and Hardware Tests
Stress testing beyond training limits (0.7 m/s pushes, +1.75 kg payload per hand) showed zero falls under pushes up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range. Even at double the payload limit, the robot withstood pushes below 0.7 m/s without falling, demonstrating high robustness margins.
On hardware, the robot stably carried a box containing a ~722.6 g payload in both hands (total hand weight ~1.2 kg/hand) across standing, half-crouching, and fully crouching heights. It also completed produce pick, transport, and place tasks on the same locomotion layer using both GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5.

### Cost of Decoupling
DUET was compared directly to a whole-body control policy controlling all 23 joints on the same G1. Neither policy fell, but whole-body control achieved an average trunk tilt of 1.7 degrees, whereas DUET exhibited 9.7 degrees—about 8 degrees larger. This happens because whole-body control can swing the arms to generate angular momentum and cancel trunk sway (momentum control). DUET's leg policy cannot control the arms, so it lacks this mechanism. This numerically confirms the cost in postural stability paid in exchange for the freedom to swap manipulation policies.

sections.heading: Why Does DUET Work? The Modularity vs. Stability Trade-off
sections.summary: DUET succeeds not by teaching the legs to coordinate with the arms, but by training them to stabilize across the entire physical disturbance envelope generated by the arms. The authors discuss the fundamental difference from whole-body control and guidelines for choosing between them.
sections.details:
What fundamentally distinguishes DUET from prior decoupled controllers is that the lower-body policy has no concept of who generates the arm targets. Instead of learning coordination with a specific manipulation policy, the legs were trained to absorb the entire physical disturbance envelope created by any arm pose or inertia change. Consequently, the lower body serves as a reusable mobility layer for arbitrary manipulation models developed independently.

As the ablations showed, the hero behind this robustness is the arm pose curriculum. Without progressively exposing the policy to vigorous arm motions, it cannot withstand them.

However, this decoupling has an explicit trade-off. The ~8 degree increase in average trunk tilt compared to whole-body control is not due to poor reward tuning; it is an architectural inevitability when the arms cannot be used as posture-control actuators. Therefore, whole-body control is superior for tasks where millimeter-level trunk stillness is paramount. But when one wants to freely swap rapidly evolving VLA models and leverage existing fixed-base manipulation assets as-is, a decoupled approach like DUET is an exceptionally practical solution.

sections.heading: Identified Challenges: Lower Grasping Success on a Mobile Base and Future Directions
sections.summary: The primary challenge is a drop in grasping success rate on hardware compared to a fixed base. Analyzing the impact of trunk tilt and latency points toward feedforward observations that anticipate arm targets one step ahead, as well as extensions to uneven terrain.
sections.details:
### Grasping Success Gap and Causes
The most prominent limitation uncovered by this study is reduced manipulation success on hardware. While GR00T N1.7 succeeded in 8 out of 10 trials on a fixed base, success dropped to 4 out of 10 on the mobile base (on top of the locomotion layer). pi0.5 achieved only 2 out of 10 successes. This degradation is likely driven by a combination of minor base tilt, standing drift, and the control frequency mismatch between the VLA (~15 Hz) and locomotion (50 Hz).

### Future Improvement Approaches
The authors outline concrete directions to bridge this gap:
- Arm Target Anticipation: While still barring the leg policy from modifying arm commands, allowing it to observe the next issued arm target one cycle in advance could shift stabilization from reactive to anticipatory.
- Fine-Tuning with Mobile Data: The VLAs used here were trained solely on fixed-base data. Fine-tuning with data collected on a moving base should improve performance.
- Broader Validation and Environments: Both models tested were fine-tuned on the same produce-handling domain. Testing with entirely different domains, such as teleoperation streams, is needed. Additionally, current testing is restricted to flat ground, making rough terrain adaptation an important next step.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Cleanly Separating Humanoids into "Mobility" and "Intelligence"
sections.summary: DUET achieves a decoupled loco-manipulation framework where changing the manipulation policy requires no changes to the balance controller. By turning the lower body into a reusable stabilization layer, it paves the way for directly linking foundation model progress to robot mobility.
sections.details:
Integrating locomotion and manipulation in humanoid robots has long sacrificed modularity for complex, simultaneous whole-body optimization. DUET breaks through this dilemma with a clear boundary: the lower body does not need to know the upper body's intent; it only needs to withstand its physical effects.

On a physical 23-DOF Unitree G1, driving two state-of-the-art VLA models—GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5—stably on the exact same locomotion policy speaks volumes about this approach's power. While a trade-off in postural stability exists, DUET provides an eminently practical engineering blueprint to unleash fast-evolving vision-language-action models and manipulation foundation models into the real world without re-engineering the robot's base.

takeaways: You do not need to retrain or redesign the locomotion controller every time you swap the manipulation policy; practical loco-manipulation is possible even with the lower body completely decoupled from arm actions.
The single most critical component in lower-body policy training is the upper-body pose curriculum; without exposure to diverse arm motions, fall rates surge.
The main cost of decoupling is increased trunk tilt (~8 degrees worse); designers must weigh this architectural constraint against the benefit of freely swapping arm policies.
Running fixed-base trained VLA models directly on a mobile base degrades grasp success rates; future progress will depend on anticipatory target observation and collecting mobile-base data.
limitations: Grasping success rates on hardware drop substantially on a mobile base compared to a fixed base (from 8/10 to 4/10 for GR00T, and 2/10 for pi0.5).
Both VLA models were fine-tuned on the same produce dataset (605 episodes), leaving full generalizability across diverse task domains unvalidated.
Because the arms cannot serve as mass dampers for whole-body balance control, average trunk tilt is roughly 8 degrees larger than with whole-body control.
Experiments were conducted exclusively on flat floors, leaving the robustness of decoupled execution on uneven terrain or stairs untested.
